issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
Kalani had spent his life working under the open sky, a roofer who took pride in the strength of his body and the sureness of his footing. Now, at forty-eight, that certainty was gone, dismantled in a single night six months ago. It had started innocently enough, a rare evening out with friends that ended with him accepting a ride from a man he’d met at the bar. He remembered the rumble of the motorcycle engine, a sound he’d once associated with freedom, and the cloying smell of alcohol on the man’s breath as he’d pulled into a darkened alley. What happened next had fractured his world. In the immediate aftermath, Kalani tried to bury it, to sweat it out on the sun-beaten rooftops he worked on every day. He told no one, least of all his wife. It was a matter of shame, a private failure he was determined to overcome through sheer force of will.

But the event would not stay buried. It began to bleed into his present, most often when he was unprepared. A news report mentioning a local assault could seize his attention, and suddenly the memory would wash over him, feeling more vivid and terrifyingly real than the living room around him. The roar of a motorcycle passing his work truck on the highway was enough to make his heart pound, instantly transporting him back to the alley. These triggers became landmines in his daily life. In response, he began to build walls. He threw himself into his work, arriving at job sites before dawn and staying long after his crew had left, believing that physical exhaustion was the only path to mental silence. This frantic busyness was a deliberate strategy; if he kept his body moving, his mind wouldn't have the space to wander back to that night.

This desperate attempt at control extended to his plate. He started restricting his diet with rigid precision, weighing his food and counting every calorie. It was a small, manageable domain where he could exert absolute authority, a stark contrast to the powerlessness he felt when a memory ambushed him. When a coworker returned from lunch with the faint smell of beer on his breath, the scent would trigger a jolt of panic, and Kalani would retreat into his routines, doubling down on his strict eating that evening or finding another project to absorb him. He also began avoiding any situation that put his body under unusual stress, turning down physically demanding side jobs he once would have welcomed, fearing the sensation of being overwhelmed.

The strategies, however, began to backfire, creating a vicious, self-sustaining loop. The long hours he worked only led to a deeper fatigue, and in those moments of exhaustion, his defenses would crumble. Driving home late one evening, a wave of pure, unattached emotion swept over him—the full grief and terror of the assault, but without any clear image. It was a terrifying ghost in his bloodstream, and the experience left him shaken for days. This consequence of his busyness made him even more hypervigilant. After such an episode, the sound of a motorcycle seemed louder, the mention of violence on the news more personal and threatening. The memory itself was sensitizing him, making the world feel dense with triggers.

His avoidance also fed the cycle. By working so hard to keep busy, he had inadvertently taught himself that stillness was dangerous, making any quiet moment a potential threat. His self-imposed physical limits at work, meant to keep him from feeling overwhelmed, sometimes left his mind too idle, creating a vacuum the memories rushed to fill. The fortress he had built was becoming a prison. His wife grew worried, commenting on his weight loss and the impenetrable wall of work he had erected between them. He was present in their home, but he was not there. It was her quiet observation one night—"I feel like I'm losing you, Kalani"—that finally broke through his defenses. He sought help not because the strategies had failed, but because they were succeeding too well, isolating him from his own life. He was terrified that the man from the alley had not just stolen one night, but was now, through these memories and fears, stealing the rest of his life as well.
